title: Oscar Wilde at the London Theater Opening: Wit, Aesthetics, and the Smoking Heckler
summary: At the triumphant opening night of 'Lady Windermere's Fan' in 1892 London, playwright Oscar Wilde disarmed an envious critic with peerless conversational elegance.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 180: நேருவின் தேநீர் அல்லது காபி
full_text:
On the evening of February 20, 1892, London’s fashionable society packed the St. James's Theatre for the premiere of Oscar Wilde’s sparkling comedy of manners, 'Lady Windermere's Fan.'

As the final curtain fell, the house erupted into thunderous, ecstatic ovations. Demands for the author echoed across the stalls. Wilde stepped onto the stage in an elegant velvet-collared coat, a green carnation pinned to his lapel, holding a lit cigarette with indolent grace.

Addressing the audience with polished theatrical detachment, Wilde remarked:
"Ladies and gentlemen, I have enjoyed this evening immensely. The actors have given an exquisite performance, and their acting was nearly as clever as the play itself."

At that moment, a disgruntled critic in the gallery seeking to embarrass Wilde shouted loudly through the hall:
"Wilde, your play is utterly dreadful! I despise it!"

A collective gasp swept through the fashionable crowd. Unfazed, Wilde raised his cigarette, smiled with effortless charm, and replied:
"My dear sir, I quite agree with you. Personally, I find the play quite dreadful myself! But what are we two against so many?"

The entire theater dissolved into helpless laughter and roaring applause. Through spontaneous self-mockery, Wilde disarmed hostility and transformed a heckler's malice into a legendary triumph of wit.
